title: How to pass this in a weekend
lead:
You have not read this course and the exam is on Tuesday. That is fine.
This book is built for exactly that. It ignores everything the exam will not ask and
teaches you, from zero, the dozen skills that answer every question. Do what it says and
you will walk in ready.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: The one idea behind this book
blocks.html: Computer Architecture looks huge but the exam is small. It reuses about a dozen ideas, over and over, with the numbers changed. So this book does not try to cover the syllabus. It works backwards from the exam: it takes the real questions as the target, then teaches every skill you need to reach them, starting from nothing. Each skill is taught so you understand why it works, not just what to write, which is the only way to stay safe when the examiner changes the numbers on you.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.tag: The habit that passes the exam
blocks.html:
Reading feels like studying and teaches you almost nothing. What puts a skill into your hands is doing it with the answer covered. So all through this book you will meet two things, and you must actually use them:

  • A Your turn box: a question with new numbers and the answer hidden under a dashed line. Cover it, work it on paper, then check. This is where the learning happens.
  • After a worked example, Now redo it: close the book and reproduce the whole solution on blank paper. If you can do that, you own the skill.

The rule: never move on from a skill until you can do its Your-turn box cold, from memory, with different numbers. That single habit is the difference between a pass and a blank page.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
Two kinds of question, and this book prepares you for both:

  • Objective questions (MCQs). Multiple choice, one right answer out of four. The lecturer has said these are coming. They test definitions and quick judgement across the whole course. Every one from the practice tests is answered and explained in Part C.
  • The written paper. The classic shape is Question One, compulsory, 30 marks, then any two of the remaining questions at 20 marks each, for 70 marks in 2 hours. Question One is where the number-crunching lives, so master it and you have half the paper before you choose anything. The whole 2025/2026 paper is worked at the back as your final mock.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
Three days, three sittings. Do the Your-turn boxes as you go, do not just read.

  • Saturday, Part A. The big picture, then all the number skills: number systems, signed numbers, floating point, and image sizing. These are pure marks and most of the numeric MCQs.
  • Sunday, Part B. The machine: instruction formats, addressing modes, CPU performance, pipelining, and memory and cache. This is the heart of Question One.
  • Monday, Part C. The last of the theory, then work the whole MCQ bank as a test, then sit the 2025/2026 paper under the clock. Spend the evening redoing anything you got wrong.

If you are short on time, the order is chosen so the earliest sections are the highest value. Never skip Part A: everything else stands on it.

title: The Big Picture
lead:
Before any sums, the shape of the whole thing. Half the objective questions
live right here: what a computer is made of, and the one distinction the examiner asks in a
dozen disguises, architecture versus organization.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: A computer runs a program by repeating three steps forever: it fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it (works out what it means), then executes it, and loops back to do it all again. That never-ending loop is the fetch, decode, execute cycle.
frames.ask: Name the three steps, in order.

frames.teach: Where do those instructions live? In memory, written as plain binary numbers, sitting right beside the data they work on. This one idea, the program and the data together in the same memory, is the stored-program (or Von Neumann) concept.
frames.ask:
Are the program and the
data kept in the same memory, or in two separate ones?

frames.teach: That is exactly what makes a computer general: change the numbers in memory and the same machine does a different job. Now look inside the processor, the CPU. Its first working part is the control unit (CU), the conductor: it fetches each instruction and sends out the control signals that make everything act at the right moment.
frames.ask:
Does the CU itself do the adding and
subtracting, yes or no?

frames.teach: The adding, subtracting, AND, OR and comparing is the job of the second part, the arithmetic and logic unit (ALU). So keep the two apart: the CU directs, the ALU calculates.
frames.ask:
Which unit actually works
out 7 + 5?

frames.teach: The CPU also keeps a few tiny, very fast stores called registers, each holding something it needs right now. The first is the program counter (PC): it holds the address of the next instruction to fetch.
frames.ask: What does the PC hold?

frames.check: the address of the next instruction.
frames.teach: Once an instruction has been fetched, it is held in the instruction register (IR) while it is decoded and run.
frames.ask:
Which register holds the instruction currently being
executed?

frames.teach: Two more registers, both for talking to memory. The memory address register (MAR) holds the address the CPU is about to read from or write to.
frames.ask: Does the MAR hold an address, or a value?

frames.teach: Its partner, the memory data register (MDR), holds the data itself going to or coming from memory. So the MAR says which location, and the MDR carries the value there.
frames.ask:
From memory, name all
four registers you have now met.

frames.teach: How do these parts reach each other and memory? Over three shared sets of wires called buses. The address bus carries which location is wanted.
frames.ask:
Which register's contents would travel out on
the address bus?

frames.teach: (the address it is holding). The data bus carries the value itself, and the control bus carries the signals that say read or write, and when.
frames.ask:
Which of the three buses carries the value
itself?

frames.teach: Now the idea the examiner asks in a dozen disguises: architecture versus organization. Computer architecture is what the machine does, as the programmer sees it; it answers "what does the computer do?"
frames.ask:
Does architecture describe what the programmer can see, or the hidden
hardware?

frames.teach: Concretely, architecture is the instruction set architecture (ISA): the instructions available, the data types, the addressing modes, the registers a program can name, the instruction formats. Rule of thumb: if a program can see it or name it, it is architecture.
frames.ask:
So is the list
of addressing modes architecture?

frames.teach: (a program chooses among them, so architecture). Its opposite is computer organization: how the machine is built to do it. It is the hidden hardware, the control signals, the buses, the memory technology, the cache, how many execution units there are; the programmer never sees it, and it decides how fast the job gets done.
frames.ask:
Architecture answers "what"; organization answers which one-word
question?

frames.teach: Here is the clean test: can a program see it or name it? Then architecture. Is it an implementation choice hidden inside? Then organization. Try it on a hard one, the size of the cache.
frames.ask:
Is cache
size architecture or organization?

frames.teach: (a hidden build choice; no program names the cache size). Because the ISA is all a program sees, two chips with the same ISA run the same programs (they are binary compatible), yet can differ wildly in speed because their organization differs; that deeper hardware realisation is the microarchitecture.
frames.ask:
If two chips share an ISA, will one compiled program
run on both?

frames.teach: One hook to lock it in for the test: architecture is the blueprint (the design); organization is the construction (how it is actually built). Same blueprint, two builders, two speeds. (There are two whole ISA styles you will meet in Part C: the reduced instruction set computer, RISC, and the complex instruction set computer, CISC.) Now slide down to the sorting card below and read both columns; most arch-vs-org questions are simply "which side is this?"

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.html:
Memorise these two lists. Most arch-vs-org MCQs are just "which side is this?"

Memory hook: architecture is the blueprint (the design); organization is the construction (how it is actually built). Same blueprint, two builders, two costs and two speeds.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Same as before: keep the page covered, read a frame, do the small task, then
slide the card down one line to check.

frames.teach: Two ways to wire memory to the CPU, and the examiner wants the difference. The first you have already met, Von Neumann: one memory and one bus shared by both instructions and data. It is simple and cheap.
frames.ask:
In a Von Neumann
machine, how many memories hold the instructions and the data?

frames.teach: (shared). That single shared path has a price: the CPU cannot fetch an instruction and read data at the very same moment, they must take turns on the one bus. That traffic jam is the well-known bottleneck.
frames.ask: What do we call the slowdown caused by sharing one path?

frames.teach: The rival design is Harvard: separate memories and separate buses, one set for instructions and another for data. It costs more hardware, since the address, data and control lines are duplicated.
frames.ask: How many separate memories does a Harvard machine use?

frames.teach: That extra hardware buys one thing: Harvard can fetch an instruction and read data at the same time, a form of parallelism, and that is its whole advantage.
frames.ask:
Which design, Von Neumann or Harvard, can fetch an
instruction and read data at once?

frames.teach: So hold the trade in your head: Von Neumann is one memory, cheap but with a shared bottleneck; Harvard is two memories, more hardware but faster because both happen together. Now look just below at the two diagrams and the how to draw each note, and practise drawing both, because the paper asks for exactly that.

blocks.label: Draw it
blocks.tag: Von Neumann vs Harvard on paper
blocks.html:
How to draw each (the paper asks for a diagram, so practise it): draw the CPU as one box. For Von Neumann, join it by a single line, the shared bus, to one Memory box holding instructions and data together. For Harvard, draw two memory boxes, an instruction memory and a data memory, and join each to the CPU by its own bus.

How to remember it: Von Neumann = one box, one bus. Harvard = two boxes, two buses; picture the two upright strokes of the letter H as the two separate memories.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: Label each as architecture (A) or organization (O): (1) the list of addressing modes, (2) the size of the cache, (3) the number of general registers a program can use, (4) the technology the main memory is built from, (5) the control signals the control unit sends.
blocks.answer: 1 A (programmer names them), 2 O (hidden size choice), 3 A (programmer-visible), 4 O (implementation), 5 O (hidden). If you can explain why for each, you have this topic.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: A bank upgrades its servers to processors with larger caches and faster RAM while keeping the same x86 instruction set. What has primarily changed?   (a) Architecture only   (b) Organization only   (c) Both   (d) Neither
blocks.answer: (b) Organization only. Same instruction set means the architecture is unchanged; larger caches and faster RAM are organization. This exact shape, "same ISA, faster hardware", appears again and again: the answer is always organization.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: A developer runs the same compiled application on two processors from different manufacturers. This is possible because both implement the same:   (a) Instruction Set Architecture   (b) Microarchitecture   (c) Control unit design   (d) Cache hierarchy
blocks.answer: (a) Instruction Set Architecture. The same binary program runs on both because they share an ISA. Their microarchitecture, control unit and cache may all differ; that is organization, and it only changes speed, not what runs.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: A processor fetches an instruction while simultaneously reading data from memory. Which architecture makes this possible?   (a) Stack   (b) CISC   (c) Von Neumann   (d) Harvard
blocks.answer: (d) Harvard. Separate instruction and data memories and buses let both happen at once. Von Neumann shares one path, so it cannot.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: When an MCQ says "same instruction set" or "same ISA" but the hardware changed, the change is organization, never architecture. And "which is visible to the programmer?" almost always points to the instruction formats / addressing modes / registers (architecture), not to caches, buses or memory technology (organization).

blocks.big:
"Architecture is the blueprint, what the machine does; organization is the
construction, how it does it."
blocks.sub: If a program can see or name it, it is architecture (the ISA); if it is a hidden build choice, it is organization. Same ISA runs the same programs. Von Neumann shares one memory; Harvard splits instructions and data so it fetches both at once.

title: Number Systems and Conversions
lead: Everything a computer holds is binary. This skill is turning numbers between binary, decimal and hexadecimal without thinking, plus the special decimal codes, and it is easy marks. We build it as a programme: many tiny steps worked through one at a time, and you check each one before the next. Go slowly and it will soon feel automatic.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do
the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a
time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: A base just means how many symbols you count with before you start a new column. Decimal is base 10: the ten symbols 0 to 9. A computer wire is only ever on or off.
frames.ask: So how many symbols does binary have?

frames.teach: (on or off), which is base 2. Binary is correct but gets very long, so we bundle it up as hexadecimal, base 16, whose symbols run 0 to 9 and then A, B, C, D, E, F.
frames.ask:
A is the first letter-symbol; what decimal
value does the hex digit A stand for?

frames.teach: Then B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14, F = 15. Next, place value: reading a number from right to left, the columns are worth base0 = 1, then base1, then base2, and so on.
frames.ask:
In hex, what is the place
value of the third column from the right?

frames.teach: So the hex columns are 1, 16, 256, 4096. Three size words before we convert: one binary digit is a bit, four bits are a nibble, and eight bits are a byte.
frames.ask:
How many bits are in a
byte?

frames.teach: (and four bits are a nibble). Now the first conversion. To turn any base into decimal, multiply each digit by its place value and add the results. Take the hex number 2F: its columns are 16 and 1, and F = 15.

That is every base-to-decimal question. The reverse, decimal to any base, divides repeatedly by the base, jots each remainder, and reads the remainders bottom to top. For 13 to binary: 13÷2 = 6 r 1, 6÷2 = 3 r 0, 3÷2 = 1 r 1, 1÷2 = 0 r 1.
frames.ask:
Read the four remainders
from the bottom up.

frames.teach: Let us prove it rather than trust it. The binary columns are 8, 4, 2, 1, and 1101 has 1-bits in the 8, 4 and 1 columns.
frames.ask: Add 8 + 4 + 1; do you land back on 13?

frames.teach: The conversion checks out. Now binary to hex. Because 16 = 24, one hex digit is exactly four bits, so group the bits into fours from the right and turn each four into one hex digit. Take 1101 0110: the right group 0110 = 4+2 = 6.
frames.ask: What hex digit is the left group 1101?

frames.teach:
(that is 8+4+1 = 13). So 1101 0110 = D6, and going the
other way you simply expand each hex digit back into its four bits.
frames.ask:
Read
on.

frames.teach: A few powers of two must be instant. 210 = 1024, which we call "1 K"; then 220 = 1 M and 230 = 1 G.
frames.ask:
How many bytes is
2<sup>10</sup>, and what one-letter name do we give it?

frames.teach: Every memory and cache question leans on these. Now the special decimal codes, where each decimal digit is kept on its own. First is BCD.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: BCD (binary coded decimal), the 8421 code, writes each decimal digit as its own 4 bits. So 59 becomes 5 = 0101 and 9 = 1001, written 0101 1001. It is a weighted code (the bit positions are worth 8, 4, 2, 1).
frames.ask:
Write the single
digit 7 in BCD.

frames.teach: (4+2+1 = 7). BCD is just the digit in plain 4-bit binary. The next code, Excess-3, takes the digit, adds 3, then writes the result in 4 bits. So 9 becomes 9+3 = 12 = 1100.
frames.ask: Write the digit 6 in Excess-3.

frames.teach: (6+3 = 9 = 1001); to decode you subtract 3. Excess-3 is non-weighted (its bits carry no fixed weight) and self-complementing.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Last, the character codes, which store text and not numbers. ASCII encodes English letters, digits and symbols in 7 or 8 bits; Unicode was introduced to cover the characters of all the world's languages.
frames.ask:
Which of the two would you
need for Chinese or Arabic letters?

frames.teach:
(it covers every language). That is every fact in
this skill. Now watch the moves used together in the two worked examples below, then sit the
recalls with the answers covered.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.tag: The three conversions, and powers of two
blocks.html:
• Any base to decimal: multiply each digit by its place value and add. In hex the places are 1, 16, 256, 4096.
  • Decimal to any base: divide repeatedly by the base, write down each remainder, then read the remainders bottom to top.
  • Binary to hex: group the bits into fours from the right, turn each group of four into one hex digit. Hex to binary is the reverse: each hex digit becomes four bits. This works because 16 = 24, so one hex digit is exactly four bits.
n012345678910
2n12481632641282565121024

Memory hook: know these powers of two cold; 210 = 1024 = "1 K", then 220 = 1 M, 230 = 1 G. Every cache and memory question needs them.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.redo: Now redo it: the only hard part is remembering 4096, 256, 16, 1. Write those four first, then multiply.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.working:
1. Group in fours from the right: 1101  0110.
  2. Each group of four to one hex digit: 1101 = 8+4+1 = 13 = D; 0110 = 4+2 = 6.
  3. Write them in order: D6.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: go backwards too. 2A7F to binary is 2=0010, A=1010, 7=0111, F=1111, giving 0010101001111111.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) Write decimal 255 in hex. (2) How many hex digits does a 20-bit binary number need? (3) A hex value shifted right by one bit is the same as which operation?
blocks.answer: (1) 255 = 15×16 + 15 = FF. (2) 20 ÷ 4 = 5 hex digits (one hex digit per four bits). (3) shifting right one bit is dividing by 2 (left one bit is times 2).

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) The Excess-3 code for decimal 9 is? (2) The Excess-3 code 0110 is which decimal digit? (3) The 8421 BCD of decimal 59 is?
blocks.answer: (1) 9 + 3 = 12 = 1100. (2) 0110 = 6, minus 3 = 3. (3) 5 = 0101, 9 = 1001, so 01011001. Remember: BCD is the digit itself in 4 bits; Excess-3 is the digit plus 3.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: Group binary into fours from the right, never the left, and pad the leftmost group with leading zeros if it is short. And do not confuse the codes: BCD is weighted (8421) and is just the digit in binary; Excess-3 is non-weighted and is the digit plus 3. "BCD" stands for binary coded decimal, nothing else.

blocks.big: "Powers of the base, right to left. And four bits make one hex digit."
blocks.sub: To decimal: digit × place, then add. To another base: divide by the base, read the remainders bottom to top. BCD is the digit in 4 bits; Excess-3 is the digit plus 3.

title: Signed Numbers
lead: This is the most asked numeric topic, and the one most people find confusing. So we do it as a programme: many tiny steps, and you check each one before moving on. Go slowly. By the last frame the moves will feel obvious.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do
the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a
time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: Start with 8 bits and no sign yet. The patterns run 0000 0000, 0000 0001, all the way up to 1111 1111. That top one, 1111 1111, is 28 − 1.
frames.ask: Write its value in decimal, then slide down.
So a top bit of 1 must mean what?

frames.teach: So just by glancing at 1010 1010 (top bit 1) you know it is a negative number. The only question left in the whole topic is which pattern to use for a given negative. The scheme real computers use is called two's complement, and the next few frames build it slowly.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Picture the 8 bits as a car odometer. It counts up 0000 0000, 0000 0001, and on to 1111 1111, then rolls back round to 0000 0000. Now turn it one step backwards from 0000 0000.
frames.ask: What pattern do you land on?

frames.teach: One step below zero. So it is natural to call 1111 1111 the value −1. Step back once more, to 1111 1110, and that is −2. Negatives are just the patterns you meet counting down from the top.
frames.ask: Counting back once more, what pattern is −3?

frames.teach: Counting all the way down would be slow, so here is the shortcut to build any negative: write the positive, flip every bit, then add 1. Try it on −1. Start with +1 = 0000 0001.
frames.ask: Flip every bit and write the result.

frames.teach: Now the second half of the shortcut.
frames.ask: Add 1 to 1111 1110. What do you get?

frames.teach: That is the same pattern the odometer gave for −1, so the shortcut is trustworthy. Say it like a chant: "flip every bit, add one." Now your turn, all by yourself: make −5 in 8 bits. Start with +5 = 0000 0101.
frames.ask: Flip, then add 1.

frames.teach: (0000 0101 flips to 1111 1010, and adding 1 gives 1111 1011.) That pattern is −5. Notice you only ever do three things: positive, flip, add one.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now the other direction: reading a negative pattern back into a number. The trick is the very same one. Take 1111 1011 (top bit 1, so it is negative). Flip it and add 1 to find its size.
frames.ask: Flip 1111 1011, add 1, and say what size you get.

frames.teach: , so the value is −5. (Flip 1111 1011 to 0000 0100, add 1 to get 0000 0101.) Writing a negative and reading one use the same move, which is why it is worth learning well.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Why did the world settle on this scheme? Two reasons. It has only one zero (just 0000 0000), and the ordinary adder does subtraction for free, because a − b is the same as a + (−b). Here is the proof. Add −5 (1111 1011) to +5 (0000 0101), and drop any carry that falls off the top.
frames.ask: What 8-bit pattern is left?
Read on.

frames.teach: Last piece: the range. Half the patterns are negative and half positive, but zero uses up one positive slot, so there is always one more negative than positive: −2n−1 to 2n−1 − 1. In 16 bits that is −32 768 to 32 767.
frames.ask: So in 8 bits the range is −128 to what?

frames.teach:
(−2<sup>7</sup> to 2<sup>7</sup> − 1 is
−128 to 127.) That is two's complement, start to finish.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Two older schemes you only need to recognise for the objective test. Sign-magnitude: a sign bit then the plain size, so −42 is 1 then 010 1010 = 1010 1010; its drawback is two zeros (+0 and −0). One's complement: negate by flipping every bit only (no add 1); it needs an end-around carry when adding and also has two zeros. Two's complement beat both by adding that 1.
frames.ask: How many zeros does sign-magnitude have?

frames.teach:
(+0 and −0). That is every idea in this topic.
Now watch all the moves used together in the worked example below, then sit it yourself with the
answer covered.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.html:
• Write a negative: positive in n bits, flip every bit, add 1.
  • Read a negative (top bit 1): flip, add 1 for the size, then put a minus in front.
  • Add: add the patterns, drop any carry off the top (no end-around carry).
  • Range in n bits: −2n−1 to 2n−1 − 1 (16 bits: −32 768 to 32 767).

Memory hook: one's complement is "flip"; two's complement is "flip and add one".

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Store −182, 487 and −1023 in a 16-bit two's-complement machine (binary and hex) and add (−182) + 487. The exam sets exactly this; you will sit it verbatim in the final mock at the back. Here is how you write it on paper, one move at a time.
blocks.working:
Given 16 bits, two's complement · −182, 487, −1023
Formula range = −215 to 215 − 1 · negative = flip the positive and add 1 · group 4 bits per hex digit
Range: -2¹⁵ to 2¹⁵ - 1  =  -32768 to 32767   (all three fit)

487  =  0000 0001 1110 0111  =  01E7

-182:  +182  =  0000 0000 1011 0110
     invert  =  1111 1111 0100 1001
        + 1  =  1111 1111 0100 1010  =  FF4A

-1023: +1023 =  0000 0011 1111 1111
     invert  =  1111 1100 0000 0000
        + 1  =  1111 1100 0000 0001  =  FC01

(-182) + 487:
     1111 1111 0100 1010
   + 0000 0001 1110 0111
   ---------------------
   1 0000 0001 0011 0001   drop the carry off the top
     0000 0001 0011 0001   =  256+32+16+1  =  305
blocks.redo: Now redo it: positive, invert, add 1, every time. Practise with −75 in 8 bits (answer 1011 0101).

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: In 8 bits: (1) what decimal is 1000 0000 in two's complement? (2) what is the two's complement of 0010 1100? (3) what decimal is 1010 1010 in sign-magnitude?

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) How many representations of zero in sign-magnitude? (2) Which scheme needs an end-around carry? (3) The one's-complement pattern 1110 0011 is which decimal? (4) Why is two's complement used?
blocks.answer: (1) two (+0 and −0). (2) one's complement. (3) top bit 1 so negative; flip 1110 0011 to 0001 1100 = 28, so −28. (4) simpler and faster hardware (one zero, and add and subtract share one circuit).

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: Reading a negative two's-complement pattern, do not just read the magnitude bits off; you must flip and add 1 first. Overflow means the true result is too big or too small for the range, not division by zero. And the end-around carry belongs to one's complement only; two's complement simply discards the top carry.

blocks.big:
"Flip and add one, to write a negative and to read one. Add the patterns, throw
away the top carry."
blocks.sub: Range in n bits: −2n−1 to 2n−1 − 1. One's complement is "flip"; two's complement is "flip and add one", which is why it has one zero and one adder for both add and subtract.

title: Floating Point, IEEE 754
lead: One 32-bit pattern has to hold both a tiny number like 0.0000001 and a huge one like 6 billion, and plain whole-number binary cannot stretch that far. The fix is a trick you already know from science class, but people find it fiddly, so we do it as a programme: many tiny steps, and you check each one before moving on. Go slowly. By the last frame the three fields will feel obvious, and both exam directions fall out of a single line.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do
the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a
time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: Here is the whole problem in one line. You have one box, exactly 32 bits wide, and it must be able to write both a tiny number like 0.0000001 and a giant one like 6,000,000,000. Plain whole-number binary, the kind you have used so far, cannot reach both ends.
frames.ask: Can plain whole-number binary write both of those in 32 bits? Yes or no?

frames.teach: It runs out of room. But you already beat this same problem in decimal, in science class: to write 6,020,000 compactly you put it as 6.02 × 106. Hidden in that little form are three separate pieces of information.
frames.ask: Name the three pieces.

frames.check:
a sign (it is positive, +), a fraction (6.02), and an exponent
(6).
frames.teach: That is all scientific notation is. Floating point does exactly this, but in base 2: a sign, a fraction, and a power of 2 instead of 10. Nothing more is going on.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: So a floating-point number is stored as those same three pieces, now called three fields, written left to right: the sign (s), then the exponent (E), then the mantissa M (which is just the fraction, also called the significand).
frames.ask: Which of the three fields sits on the far left?

frames.teach: Now their sizes. Single precision is 32 bits, split as 1 sign bit, then 8 exponent bits.
frames.ask: That leaves how many bits for the mantissa, to reach 32?

frames.teach: (1 + 8 + 23 = 32.) You only need to recognise the bigger size: double precision is 64 bits, split 1 + 11 + 52. Everything from here uses single precision.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: One preparation step, called normalising. In decimal you insist on exactly one non-zero digit before the point (6.02, never 60.2 or 0.602). In binary you do the same: slide the point until the number reads 1.something × 2e. Since the only non-zero binary digit there can be is 1,
frames.ask:
what single thing does a normalised
binary number always start with?

frames.teach: Always. And here is the first trick that helps: because it is always "1.", actually storing that 1 would waste a bit on something you already know for certain. So it is left out and just assumed. This is the famous hidden 1.
frames.ask:
When you READ a stored pattern back, what must you put in front of
the mantissa?

frames.teach: Put the hidden 1 back before you read. And going the other way, when you write a number you drop that leading 1 and keep only what follows the point. It costs nothing and buys you one extra bit of precision for free.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now the second trick, the one that trips up most beginners: the bias. The exponent can be negative (for a tiny number like 2−3) or positive (for a big one). Rather than give the exponent its own sign bit, we add a fixed number, the bias, so the stored exponent is always a positive count. The bias is 127 for single (1023 for double). It is like storing temperatures as "degrees above −127", so a minus sign is never needed.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: So the stored exponent field is the true exponent plus 127. To undo that and get the true exponent back, you simply subtract the bias again. Suppose a pattern has an exponent field of 130.
frames.ask: What is its true exponent?

frames.teach: (130 − 127 = 3.) That is the whole method on one line, so learn it: value = ± 1.M × 2(exponent field − 127). Both exam directions fall straight out of it.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: One last reading skill: turning the mantissa into a number. After the hidden "1.", each mantissa bit is a smaller and smaller fraction: the first bit is worth 1/2, the next 1/4, the next 1/8. So a stored mantissa of 100… reads as 1.1 in binary, which is 1 + 1/2.
frames.ask: What is 1 + 1/2 in decimal?

frames.teach: Now decode a whole real pattern, one field at a time. Take sign bit 1, exponent field 130, mantissa 100…. The sign bit 1 means negative, the field 130 gives e = 3 (you just did that), and the mantissa gives 1.M = 1.5. First the power:
frames.ask: what is 2<sup>3</sup>?

frames.teach: Now hang the sign and the mantissa on it: value = −1.5 × 23 = −1.5 × 8.
frames.ask: Finish it: what number is that?

frames.teach: You just decoded a floating-point pattern by hand. Now prove the bias to yourself: to STORE that same exponent of 3 you would go the other way and do 3 + 127.
frames.ask: What exponent field would you store?

frames.teach:
The very field you started from, so the bias undoes
itself cleanly, going in and coming out. That is every idea in the topic: three fields, normalise to
1.something, hide the leading 1, and shift the exponent by the bias. Now watch all the moves used
together in the worked example below (it decodes this exact pattern, C1400000), then sit the two
"Your turn" boxes with the answer covered.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.html:
• Decimal to IEEE (single): (1) sign bit from the sign. (2) Convert the magnitude to binary. (3) Normalise to 1.something × 2e by moving the point. (4) Exponent field = e + 127, in 8 bits. (5) Mantissa = the "something" after the point, padded with zeros to 23 bits (the leading 1 is dropped, it is the hidden 1). (6) Put the 32 bits together and group in fours for hex.
  • IEEE (hex) to decimal: (1) write the 32 bits, split as 1 / 8 / 23. (2) Sign bit gives the sign. (3) Real exponent e = exponent field − 127. (4) Value = ± 1.M in binary × 2e (remember to put the hidden 1 back).

Memory hook: "sign, exponent, mantissa", and the exponent is always stored plus the bias, read minus the bias.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Convert C1400000 (single precision) to decimal. This is the X the exam sets in Question 4a; you will sit it verbatim in the final mock.
blocks.working:
Given C1400000h, single precision
Formula value = (−1)sign × 1.M × 2(exp field − 127)
C1400000 = 1 10000010 100 0000...
  sign 1  ->  negative
  exp field 1000 0010 = 130,  e = 130 - 127 = 3
  mantissa 1.100... = 1 + 1/2 = 1.5
  value = -1.5 x 2³ = -1.5 x 8 = -12
blocks.redo: Now redo it: exponent field minus 127, then read 1.M as a binary fraction (first bit a half, next a quarter).

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: Encode +6.0 in single precision. (Hint: 6 in binary is 110; normalise it.)

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) How many exponent bits in single precision? (2) The bias in double precision? (3) How many bits is double precision? (4) A floating-point number is stored as which order of fields?
blocks.answer: (1) 8. (2) 1023. (3) 64. (4) sign, then exponent, then mantissa (the exam phrases the answer as "sign, mantissa, exponent", meaning those three parts with the sign first; the true field order on the chip is sign, exponent, mantissa).

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: Do not forget the bias: the exponent you compute is e + 127 going in, and field − 127 coming out. And the leading 1 is hidden, so when you read the mantissa put a "1." in front of it. Single precision has range about 10±38; double about 10±308.

blocks.big:
"Sign, exponent, mantissa. Add the bias going in, take the bias coming out, and
always hide the leading 1."
blocks.sub: Single precision is 32 bits = 1 + 8 + 23, bias 127. One line runs both directions: value = ± 1.M × 2(field − 127).

title: Image and Memory Sizing
lead: A small, reliable question: how much memory a picture needs. One formula and a couple of unit facts, and the marks are yours. We build it as a programme of tiny steps, worked through one at a time, so cover the page and check yourself as you go.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do
the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a
time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: A bitmap image (also called raster) is a grid of tiny squares, and each square stores its own colour as a few bits.
frames.ask:
So a bitmap picture is built
out of what?

frames.teach: A vector image is different: it stores the shapes as maths (lines and curves), so it can be scaled to any size with no loss of quality.
frames.ask:
A logo that must be blown up to billboard size with no blur, bitmap or
vector?

frames.teach:
(the maths redraws it crisply at any size). A
photograph, with its continuous shades, is stored as a bitmap.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now colour depth, the number of bits each pixel uses. Monochrome (black or white only) needs 1 bit per pixel; greyscale is often 8 bits; full colour is 24 bits.
frames.ask: How many bits per pixel does a monochrome image use?

frames.teach:
(only two states, black or white). Now the size
formula. The number of bits in a bitmap is width in pixels × height in pixels × bits per
pixel. Picture a small 100 by 50 pixel monochrome image.
To turn bits into bytes, divide by 8.

So the whole chain is pixels across ×
pixels down × bits per pixel, then ÷ 8 for bytes.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Often the size is given in inches at a certain dpi (dots per inch). Get the pixels first: pixels = inches × dpi, the same way for width and for height. Take 2 inches at 300 dpi.
frames.ask: How many pixels is 2 × 300?

frames.teach:
Do that for the width and the height, then feed
the two pixel counts into the size formula as before.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: One last caution. A megabyte can mean 1024 × 1024 bytes or a plain one million bytes, and the two give slightly different answers, so always say which you used. That is the whole skill. Now work the example below with the answer covered.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: An image is 17.12 inches by 9.45 inches at 250 dpi, 1 bit per pixel. Find its memory in megabytes. The exam sets exactly this; sit it verbatim in the final mock.
blocks.working:
Given 17.12 in × 9.45 in · 250 dpi · 1 bit per pixel
Formula pixels = inches × dpi (both ways) · bytes = pixels × bits / 8 · MB = bytes / 1024 / 1024
pixels across = 17.12 x 250 = 4280
pixels down   =  9.45 x 250 = 2362.5
total pixels  = 4280 x 2362.5 = 10 111 500
bytes = 10 111 500 / 8 = 1 263 937.5
MB    = 1 263 937.5 / 1024 / 1024 = 1.21 MB
blocks.answer:
10 111 500 pixels × 1 bit = 1 263 937.5 bytes ≈ 1.21 MB. Say
which megabyte you used (1024 twice gives 1.21; a million gives about 1.26).
blocks.redo: Now redo it: pixels first, times the bits per pixel, divide by 8, then by 1024 twice.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) How many bits per pixel for a monochrome bitmap? (2) A logo must be enlarged to billboard size without losing quality: bitmap or vector? (3) Photographs are best represented as?
blocks.answer: (1) 1 bit (two states). (2) vector (scales with no quality loss). (3) bitmap (a photo is a grid of continuous-tone pixels).

blocks.big: "Pixels = inches × dpi. Bits = pixels × depth. Bytes = bits ÷ 8."
blocks.sub: For megabytes, divide by 1024 twice, and say which megabyte you used. Vector scales with no quality loss; a bitmap does not. Monochrome is 1 bit per pixel.

title: Instruction Sets and Formats
lead:
What a machine instruction is, the kinds there are, and the four
"address" formats the paper asks you to write a program in. Plus the counting question the
objective test likes.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do
the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a
time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: A machine instruction is one small command for the CPU. It always names an operation to carry out, for example ADD. The part that says which operation is called the opcode.
frames.ask: Name the part of an instruction that says which operation to do.

frames.teach: Sitting beside the opcode are zero or more operands: the things the operation works on. In ADD A, B the opcode is ADD, and A and B are the operands. (Each operand also carries an addressing mode saying where it is; that is the next section.)
frames.ask: In ADD A, B, what are A and B called?

frames.teach: Opcode and operands are just bit fields packed side by side. The fixed layout of those fields is the instruction format.
frames.ask: What word means the layout of the bit fields in an instruction?

frames.teach: (the instruction format). And the whole collection of instructions one CPU understands is called its instruction set. That is the vocabulary. Now the kinds of instructions.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: There are four main types. First, data transfer: LOAD, STORE, MOVE. These move data between registers and memory, and a LOAD in particular reads from memory into the CPU.
frames.ask: Does LOAD read from memory, or write to it?

frames.teach: Second, arithmetic and logic: ADD, SUB, AND, OR. This is the ALU's work. Third, input/output: talk to devices.
frames.ask: Which unit does the ADD and AND work?
Which type changes the order instructions run in?

frames.teach: Now the four address formats. This is only a count: how many operand addresses each instruction names. We go from most to fewest.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Three-address names both sources and the destination in one instruction, e.g. ADD X, A, B meaning X = A + B. Because each instruction does so much, you need the fewest of them.
frames.ask: How many addresses does ADD X, A, B name?

frames.teach: Two-address drops the separate destination; the destination doubles as one source, e.g. ADD A, B means A = A + B.
frames.ask: After ADD A, B, where has the result gone?

frames.teach: One-address works through a single register called the accumulator: LOAD a value in, do the operation, then STORE the result out. Only one address is named each time.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Zero-address names no address at all. It is a stack machine: you PUSH operands onto the stack, and ADD simply pops the top two and pushes their sum.
frames.ask: Which of the four formats is the stack machine?

frames.teach: Now the trade-off across all four. Fewer addresses means each instruction is shorter, but you need more of them.
frames.ask: Which format gives the shortest program (fewest instructions)?

frames.teach: And the other end: zero-address gives the longest program (most instructions), though each one is tiny. You will write one expression in all four formats in the worked example below.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach:
Now the counting question the objective test likes. To size a program in bytes,
count each instruction and add up, using: bytes per instruction = opcode bytes + (number of
addresses × bytes per address).
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: A single instruction's total length is just its fields added together. Take an 8-bit opcode, a 6-bit register field and an 18-bit address field.
frames.ask: Add them; what is the total length in bits?

frames.teach: (8 + 6 + 18 = 32.) When every instruction is the same size it is called fixed-length; these decode faster and are used by RISC. Variable-length instructions are used by CISC.
frames.ask: Which style, fixed or variable, is faster to decode?

frames.teach: Last one: to fit more opcodes into the same instruction length, you give the opcode more bits (and the operands fewer). That is every idea here. Now watch one expression written in all four formats in the worked example below, then sit the recall with the answer covered.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.html:
bytes per instruction = opcode bytes + (number of addresses × bytes per address)

A single instruction's total length is its fields added: an 8-bit opcode + a 6-bit register field + an 18-bit address field = 32 bits. Fixed-length (all one size) decodes faster and is used by RISC; variable-length by CISC. More opcodes in the same length means giving the opcode more bits.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.working:
The same expression in each format. Watch the instruction count climb as the number of addresses drops.

Three-address (shortest, 3 instructions):

ADD  T, A, B      ; T = A + B
ADD  X, C, D      ; X = C + D
MUL  X, T, X      ; X = T * X

Two-address (destination is also a source):

MOV  T, A
ADD  T, B         ; T = A + B
MOV  X, C
ADD  X, D         ; X = C + D
MUL  X, T         ; X = X * T

One-address (one accumulator, AC):

LOAD  A
ADD   B           ; AC = A + B
STORE T
LOAD  C
ADD   D           ; AC = C + D
MUL   T           ; AC = AC * T
STORE X

Zero-address (stack, most instructions but each is tiny):

PUSH A   PUSH B   ADD      ; A + B on the stack
PUSH C   PUSH D   ADD      ; C + D on the stack
MUL                       ; (A+B) * (C+D)
POP  X

The bigger version, X = ((A×B) + C/D) / (F×G + J×K), is Question 4b on the 2025/2026 paper and is in your final mock at the back.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) Which format is used by stack machines? (2) Which instruction category changes the program's execution sequence? (3) An instruction has an 8-bit opcode, a 6-bit register field and an 18-bit address field: total length? (4) Which is NOT defined by the ISA: addressing modes, instruction formats, internal ALU implementation, or visible registers?
blocks.answer: (1) zero-address (operands on the stack top). (2) control transfer (branch/jump/call). (3) 8 + 6 + 18 = 32 bits. (4) internal ALU implementation (that is organization, not the programmer-visible ISA).

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: "Zero-address" goes with the stack and operands on top of the stack; do not mix it up with three-address (the shortest program). And the ISA defines what the programmer sees (formats, modes, registers), never how the ALU is wired inside.

blocks.big:
"Opcode says what; operands say what to. Fewer addresses, shorter instructions
but more of them."
blocks.sub:
Three-address is the shortest program; zero-address (a stack) the longest. Bytes =
opcode + (number of addresses × bytes each). Fixed-length decodes faster (RISC); variable-length
is CISC.

title: Addressing Modes
lead:
An address field in an instruction does not always hold the operand directly.
The addressing mode says how to turn that field into the real location, the effective address,
and then the operand. Learn the six or seven modes as "how many hops through memory", and this
is easy marks on both the paper and the objective test.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do
the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a
time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: Here is the one idea behind every addressing mode. An instruction carries an address field, but that field does not always hold the operand you want. The mode is the rule for turning the field into the real place, and then the operand.
frames.ask: What does the addressing mode tell you how to find?

frames.check: the real location, then the operand.
frames.teach: Two names to fix first. The real location of the operand is the effective address, or EA. And M[x] is shorthand for "the value stored at address x", so M[1200] is the value sitting at address 1200.
frames.ask: In words, what does M[4500] mean?

frames.teach: We will grade every mode by one question: how many hops through memory does it take to reach the operand? We start with the fewest.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Immediate mode. The operand is a plain constant written inside the instruction itself, so you never touch memory to fetch it.
frames.ask: How many memory hops does immediate mode need?

frames.teach: Needing no memory access, immediate is the fastest way to supply a constant. Next, direct mode: the field is the address, so EA = the field and the operand = M[field], one hop into memory.
frames.ask: Direct mode reads memory how many times?

frames.teach: (one hop). Indirect mode adds one more hop. Now the field holds the address of the address: first EA = M[field], then the operand = M[ M[field] ]. That is two hops, a pointer to a pointer.
frames.ask: How many hops does indirect mode take?

frames.teach:
Because indirect follows an address that is itself
stored in memory, it is exactly what you need to chase pointers, for example down a linked list.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Two modes lean on a register instead of memory. Register mode: the operand sits in a named register, so no memory hop at all. Register indirect: the register holds an address, so the operand is M[register], one hop.
frames.ask:
In register-indirect, is the operand in the register, or at the address the
register holds?

frames.check: at the address the register holds.
frames.teach: Last group, the "add" modes; each adds something to the field to make the EA. Relative: EA = PC + field. Indexed: EA = index register + field. Base: EA = base register + displacement.
frames.ask: What does relative mode add to the field?

frames.teach: Now put it to work on one running example. Take PC = 7000, R1 = 1500, address field = 1200, and memory holds M[1200] = 4500, M[4500] = 999, M[1500] = 6000. Keep these in view. First, direct (EA = field, operand = M[field]).
frames.ask: Give the direct operand.

frames.teach: (EA = 1200, operand = M[1200] = 4500.) Now indirect on the same field: first EA = M[1200], then operand = M[that].
frames.ask: Work both hops and give the indirect operand.

frames.teach: (EA = M[1200] = 4500, then operand = M[4500] = 999.) Now register indirect with R1 = 1500: the register holds the address, so operand = M[R1].
frames.ask: Give the register-indirect operand.

frames.teach: (R1 = 1500, so operand = M[1500] = 6000.) Finally relative, an add-mode: EA = PC + field, with PC = 7000 and field = 1200.
frames.ask: Give the relative EA.

frames.teach:
(7000 + 1200 = 8200. The table gives no M[8200], so
you would report the EA and never invent a value.)
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now the whole thing on one card. Immediate = the operand is in the instruction (zero hops). Direct = one hop. Indirect = two hops. And the add-modes (relative, indexed, base) add a register or the PC to the field first, then read there.
frames.ask: Order these by hops, fewest first: direct, immediate, indirect.

frames.teach:
That is every mode
you need. Now study the worked example and recall below, which run this exact PC = 7000, R1 = 1500,
field = 1200 example, and sit them with the answers covered.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.html:
The effective address (EA) is where the operand really is; M[x] means "the value stored at address x". Each mode is one more hop than the last:

ModeEffective addressOperand is
Immediatenonethe value inside the instruction (a constant)
DirectEA = the address fieldM[address field]
IndirectEA = M[address field]M[ M[address field] ]
Registernonethe value in the named register
Register indirectEA = contents of the registerM[register]
Relative (PC-relative)EA = PC + address fieldM[PC + field]
IndexedEA = index register + address fieldM[index + field]
BaseEA = base register + displacementM[base + displacement]

Memory hook: immediate = in the instruction (zero hops, fewest memory accesses); direct = one hop; indirect = two hops (a pointer to a pointer). Register indirect uses a register as the pointer; relative, indexed and base all add something to the field.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem:
PC = 7000, R1 = 1500, address field = 1200. Memory holds: M[1200] = 4500, M[4500] = 999, M[1500] = 6000. Give the EA and operand for each mode. The exam sets exactly this; sit it verbatim in the final mock.

ModeEffective addressOperand
Immediatenonethe field itself = 1200
Direct1200M[1200] = 4500
IndirectM[1200] = 4500M[4500] = 999
RegisternoneR1 = 1500
Register indirectR1 = 1500M[1500] = 6000
RelativePC + 1200 = 8200M[8200], not in the given table
blocks.answer:
Immediate 1200; Direct 4500; Indirect 999; Register 1500; Register
indirect 6000; Relative EA 8200. If the table has no entry for an EA, say so, do not invent a
value.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: follow the hops. Direct reads memory once, indirect twice, the "add" modes add a register to the field first.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) R1 = 2000, M[2000] = 500. Register-indirect operand? (2) Instruction address 500, displacement +30, PC-relative EA? (3) R2 = 300 (index), displacement 20, indexed EA? (4) Base register 4000, displacement 120, base EA? (5) Address 700, M[700] = 1500, M[1500] = 60. Indirect operand?

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) A constant is embedded in the instruction: which mode? (2) Which mode needs the fewest memory accesses? (3) Which mode best suits following pointers in a linked list?
blocks.answer: (1) immediate. (2) immediate (the operand is already in the instruction, no memory hop). (3) indirect (it dereferences a pointer, which is exactly what a linked list needs).

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: When a question gives you M[EA], read what it asks: the effective address is the location, the operand is the value there. For indexed, base and relative modes, you add the register or PC to the field to get the EA; the value stored at that EA is the operand, one further hop.

blocks.big: "Count the hops through memory: immediate 0, direct 1, indirect 2."
blocks.sub: The effective address is the place; the operand is the value at it. Indexed, base and relative all add a register or the PC to the field to get the effective address.

title: CPU Performance
lead:
How fast a processor runs is a calculation, not a mystery. Two formulas do
almost everything: the CPU-time equation and Amdahl's law. This is the most heavily weighted
numeric topic on the recent paper.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: Everything about processor speed comes from one equation. A program's running time is three numbers multiplied together: CPU time = IC × CPI × T. IC is the instruction count (how many instructions actually run), CPI is the average cycles per instruction, and T is how long one clock cycle lasts.
frames.ask: Say what each of the three, IC, CPI and T, stands for, then slide down.

frames.check: instruction count, average cycles per instruction, clock cycle time.
frames.teach: The clock rate you see advertised (say 4 GHz) is cycles per second, so one cycle lasts T = 1 / clock rate.
frames.ask: Put that in place of T and write CPU time using clock rate.

frames.teach: So a faster clock shortens the time, but a smaller instruction count or a smaller CPI does too. All three matter.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Look closer at CPI. Instructions are not all equal: a register add may take 1 cycle, an indirect memory access 4. The average CPI weights each type by how often it appears, adding up (fraction of the type × its cycles) over all types. The fractions must add to 1.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Try a tiny one. A program is 70% simple instructions at 1 cycle each and 30% at 3 cycles each.
frames.ask: Work out the average CPI: (0.70 × 1) + (0.30 × 3).

frames.teach: (0.70 × 1 = 0.70, and 0.30 × 3 = 0.90, giving 1.60.) Notice 0.70 and 0.30 add to 1, exactly as the fractions must.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: A second speed measure is MIPS, millions of instructions per second: MIPS = clock rate / (CPI × 10<sup>6</sup>). A faster clock or a lower CPI both raise it.
frames.ask: If the clock rate is 2 × 10<sup>9</sup> and CPI is 2, find the MIPS.

frames.teach: (2 × 10<sup>9</sup> divided by (2 × 10<sup>6</sup>) gives 1000.)
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: When you improve something, always measure the gain against the OLD time: improvement = (old − new) / old.
frames.ask: Old time 200, new time 150: what fraction is the improvement?

frames.teach: ((200 − 150) / 200 = 50 / 200 = 0.25.) Divide by the old value, never the new.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: So is a chip fast just because its clock is fast? No. Because time = (IC × CPI) / clock rate, the instruction count and CPI count just as much, and behind CPI sit cache behaviour, branch prediction and instruction-level parallelism.
frames.ask: Name one reason a high-clock chip can still be slow.

frames.teach: (or a large instruction count, or poor cache or branch behaviour). That is why "judge a processor by clock frequency only" is wrong.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now the second big formula, Amdahl's law. Suppose you speed up only PART of a task. The part you did not touch still takes its full time, so it caps the gain. Let f be the fraction of the original time spent in the part you improve, and let s be how many times faster you make that part.
frames.ask: In your own words, what does f stand for?

frames.check: the fraction of the time spent in the part you speed up.
frames.teach: That part's time shrinks from f to f / s, while the rest, (1 − f), is unchanged. If the whole job was time 1, the new time is (1 − f) + f / s, and speedup is old over new.
frames.ask: Write the speedup S.

frames.teach: Old time 1 on top, new time (1 − f) + f / s on the bottom.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Push s as large as you like, so f / s shrinks towards 0. Then S climbs only as far as 1 / (1 − f), because the untouched (1 − f) never goes away. Memory hook: the slow part you left alone sets the ceiling.
frames.ask: With f = 0.85, what is the best speedup possible, even with an infinite s?

frames.teach: (1 / (1 − 0.85) = 1 / 0.15 = 6.67.) Now a real, finite case: a cache 10 times faster (s = 10) that the CPU hits 85% of the time (f = 0.85). First find the new time, (1 − f) + f / s.

frames.ask: Finish it: what is S?

frames.teach: (1 / 0.235 = 4.26.) Far below the cache's 10 times, because the 15% of slow accesses dominate, which is exactly Amdahl's point. The reference card and the two worked examples below sit both of these formulas; do them with the answers covered.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.tag: the performance formulas on one card
blocks.html:
• CPU time = IC × CPI × T = (IC × CPI) / clock rate (since T = 1 / clock rate).
  • Average CPI = Σ(fraction of each type × its cycles), and the fractions add to 1.
  • MIPS = clock rate / (CPI × 106).
  • Improvement = (old − new) / old, always against the old time.
  • Amdahl's law: S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f / s), ceiling 1 / (1 − f).

Memory hook: the slow part you left alone sets the ceiling, no matter how fast you make the rest.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: One million instructions, by addressing mode: Register 40% at 1 cycle, Immediate 20% at 1, Direct 15% at 2, Indirect 10% at 4, Indexed 10% at 3, Relative 5% at 2. Find the average CPI and total cycles; then optimise indirect to 2 cycles and give the improvement. The exam sets exactly this; sit it verbatim in the final mock.
blocks.working:
Given IC = 1 000 000 · the share and cycle cost of each mode
Formula CPI = Σ(fraction × cycles) · total = IC × CPI · improvement = (old − new) / old
Avg CPI = 0.40x1 + 0.20x1 + 0.15x2 + 0.10x4 + 0.10x3 + 0.05x2
        = 0.40 + 0.20 + 0.30 + 0.40 + 0.30 + 0.10
        = 1.70

Total cycles = 1 000 000 x 1.70 = 1 700 000

Indirect 4 -> 2:  new CPI = 1.70 - 0.10x4 + 0.10x2
                          = 1.70 - 0.20
                          = 1.50

Improvement = (1.70 - 1.50) / 1.70 = 0.20 / 1.70 = 11.76%
blocks.answer: CPI 1.70; total cycles 1 700 000; new CPI 1.50; improvement 11.76%.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: weighted average, then recompute with the one changed cost.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: A cache is 10 times faster than main memory, and the CPU finds what it needs in cache 85% of the time. Find the overall speedup. The exam sets exactly this; sit it verbatim in the final mock.
blocks.working:
Given f = 0.85 (cache hits) · s = 10
Formula S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/s)
S = 1 / ((1 - 0.85) + 0.85/10)
  = 1 / (0.15 + 0.085)
  = 1 / 0.235
  = 4.26
blocks.answer:
S = 4.26, far below 10, because the 15% of slow accesses dominate. That
is exactly Amdahl's point.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: the "10 times faster" is s, not the answer; only the 85% gets divided by s, the other 15% stays at full cost.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) A benchmark runs 12 billion instructions at 4 GHz with an average CPI of 1.5. Execution time? (2) Why should performance not be judged by clock frequency alone?
blocks.answer: (1) time = (IC × CPI) / clock rate = (12×109 × 1.5) / (4×109) = 18 / 4 = 4.5 seconds. (2) because it also depends on CPI, instruction count, cache behaviour and instruction-level parallelism, not clock speed by itself.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: Improvement is measured against the old time, (old − new)/old, not the new. In Amdahl's law, f is the fraction sped up and only that part is divided by s; a "10 times faster" cache with 85% hits gives about 4.26, not 10.

blocks.big:
"Time = IC × CPI × T. In Amdahl's law, the slow part you leave alone sets
the ceiling."
blocks.sub: Improvement is measured against the old time, (old − new)/old. However fast you make the rest, speedup can never beat 1/(1 − f). CPI is a weighted average of the cycles.

title: Pipelining and Hazards
lead:
Overlapping instructions so several are in progress at once, like a laundry
that washes one load while drying the last. It speeds the processor up, and the paper asks you
to compute that speedup and to name the hazards that get in the way.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: Pipelining means overlapping instructions so several are in progress at once. Picture a laundry: you do not wait for one load to wash, dry and fold before starting the next, because the moment the first load moves to the dryer the second goes into the washer. A processor overlaps its instructions the same way.
frames.ask: What everyday process is pipelining most like?

frames.teach: (or any assembly line). To overlap them, we split each instruction into stages, called k stages. A common five are IF (instruction fetch), ID (instruction decode), EX (execute), MEM (memory access) and WB (write back). Each stage is its own hardware, so five instructions can each sit in a different stage at the same moment.
frames.ask: Name the five stages in order.

frames.teach: Without a pipeline, instruction 2 cannot start until instruction 1 has passed through every stage. With a pipeline, the instant an instruction leaves a stage the next one enters it, so once the pipe is full one instruction finishes every clock cycle.
frames.ask: Once the pipe is full, how many instructions complete per clock cycle?

frames.teach: That steady one-per-cycle output is the whole payoff. Now, how long is one clock cycle? Every stage must finish inside it, so the cycle is set by the slowest stage plus a small latch delay between stages, never the average and never the sum.
frames.ask: If the stages take 60, 50, 90, 80 ns with a 10 ns latch, what is the cycle time?

frames.teach: (The slowest stage is 90 ns, plus the 10 ns latch, giving 100 ns.)
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now the time for n instructions. The first takes k cycles to fill the pipe; after that one more finishes every cycle, so n instructions take (k + n − 1) cycles, which you then multiply by the cycle time.
frames.ask: With k = 4 stages and n = 500 tasks, how many cycles is that?
Read on.

frames.teach: Without the pipeline each instruction needs its full one-instruction time, the sum of the stage times, here 60 + 50 + 90 + 80 = 280 ns. The speedup is that one-instruction time divided by the cycle time, and it can never exceed k, the number of stages.
frames.ask: Divide 280 ns by the 100 ns cycle to get the speedup.

frames.teach: (280 / 100 = 2.8, below the ceiling of k = 4 stages.) For a whole batch you compare totals instead: 500 × 280 = 140 000 ns without a pipeline, against 50 300 ns with one. The reference card and the two worked examples below sit exactly these; do them with the answers covered.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.html:
• Cycle time = slowest stage + latch delay.
  • Pipelined time for n tasks = (k + n − 1) × cycle time. (It takes k cycles to fill with the first task, then one more cycle for each of the other n − 1.)
  • Non-pipelined time for n tasks = n × (time for one instruction). One instruction takes the sum of all the stage times, or the given per-instruction time.
  • Speedup = non-pipelined time / pipelined time. Its ceiling is k.

Memory hook: "k + n − 1", and the clock runs at the slowest stage, never the average.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: A pipeline has 4 phases of 60, 50, 90, 80 ns, with a 10 ns latch delay. Find the cycle time, the one-task time, the speedup, and the times for 500 tasks. The exam sets exactly this; sit it verbatim in the final mock.
blocks.working:
Given 4 phases 60, 50, 90, 80 ns · latch 10 ns · 500 tasks
Formula cycle = slowest + latch · pipe(n) = (k + n − 1) × cycle · seq(n) = n × Σphases · speedup = Σphases / cycle
Cycle    = max(60,50,90,80) + 10 = 90 + 10 = 100 ns
One task = 60 + 50 + 90 + 80 = 280 ns
Speedup  = 280 / 100 = 2.8
Pipe 500 = (4 + 500 - 1) x 100 = 503 x 100 = 50 300 ns
Seq 500  = 500 x 280 = 140 000 ns
blocks.answer:
Cycle 100 ns; one task 280 ns; speedup 2.8; 500 tasks pipelined
50 300 ns against sequential 140 000 ns.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: A non-pipelined processor takes 60 ns per instruction. Redesigned as a 6-stage pipeline with a 12 ns cycle time, running 50 instructions. Find both times and the speedup. (This is the one question on the revision deck that is not on any past paper, so learn it fresh.)
blocks.working:
Given non-pipelined 60 ns/instruction · k = 6 stages · cycle 12 ns · n = 50
Formula non-pipe = n × time/instruction · pipe = (k + n − 1) × cycle · speedup = non-pipe / pipe
Without pipelining = 50 x 60 = 3000 ns
With pipelining    = (6 + 50 - 1) x 12
                   = 55 x 12
                   = 660 ns      (fill 6x12=72, then 49x12=588)
Speedup            = 3000 / 660 = 4.55
blocks.answer: Without pipelining 3000 ns; with pipelining 660 ns; speedup 4.55.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: n × per-instruction time without, (k + n − 1) × cycle with, then divide.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: Overlapping is not free: sometimes two instructions in the pipe clash, and a clash is called a hazard. There are three kinds, and you must be able to name them. The first is the structural hazard, where two instructions need the same piece of hardware in the same cycle (one memory wanted for a fetch and a data access at once).
frames.ask: How do you remove a structural hazard?

frames.teach: (for example, separate instruction and data memories, so each instruction has its own). The second kind is the data hazard: an instruction needs a result that an earlier instruction has not written yet. We name its three types by the order in which two instructions touch the same register.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: RAW (read after write) is the true dependency: the second instruction reads a register the first has not written yet. It is eased by forwarding, which feeds the result straight from where it is produced to where it is needed, before the write-back stage.
frames.ask: Which of the three data hazards is the real dependency?

frames.teach: The other two, WAR (write after read) and WAW (write after write), are only naming clashes over the same register, not true data flow.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: When forwarding cannot deliver the value in time, the pipeline must stall: it inserts a bubble, an idle cycle, until the value is ready.
frames.ask: What is the idle cycle a stall inserts called?

frames.teach: The third kind is the control hazard: a branch changes which instruction runs next, but the pipe has already fetched the ones right after the branch. It is eased by branch prediction and speculative execution, whose whole purpose is to reduce control-hazard stalls.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now classify one pair. The first instruction writes R3, and the second instruction reads R3. The shared register is R3, and the order is write then read.
frames.ask: Which data hazard is that?

frames.teach: (write then read is exactly read-after-write). That is every hazard idea in place. The box just below shows how to draw the pipeline timing diagram the paper sometimes asks for; after it, sit the two "your turn" boxes with the answers covered.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: How to draw the timing (cycle) diagram
blocks.html:
The paper sometimes says "draw the pipeline timing diagram" or "draw the cycle diagram". It is always the same grid, and you draw it the same way every time:

  • Cycles across the top (1, 2, 3, ...), one instruction per row down the side.
  • In each cell write the stage that instruction is in that cycle: IF, ID, EX, (MEM), WB. Some papers add an operand fetch (OF) stage between ID and EX; use whatever stages the question names.
  • Each instruction begins its IF one cycle after the instruction above it.
  • A multi-cycle execute (say a 3-cycle multiply or a 6-cycle divide) writes EX in that many cells in a row, and everything behind it slides right.
  • A stall (waiting for a hazard to clear, or for a busy stage) is a gap you mark with a bubble, written --.

The total number of cycles is simply the column where the last instruction reaches WB. That is your answer to "how many cycles".

How to remember it: "cycles across, instructions down, stages in the boxes, count to the last WB." A long EX pushes; a stall is a --. (You will draw exactly this for Question Two and Question Three in the final mock.)

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: Find the one register on both lines and read its order. (i) R3 ← R1 op R2, then R5 ← R3 op R4. (ii) R3 ← R1 op R2, then R1 ← R4 op R5. (iii) R3 ← R1 op R2, then R3 ← R6 op R7.
blocks.answer: (i) R3 is written then read, so RAW. (ii) R1 is read then written, so WAR. (iii) R3 is written then written, so WAW. Only RAW is a real data dependency; the other two are naming clashes.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) The main objective of branch prediction and speculative execution is to? (2) A read-after-write clash is eased by which technique?
blocks.answer: (1) reduce pipeline stalls caused by control hazards (keep the pipe full across branches). (2) forwarding (feed the result straight to where it is needed).

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: The clock runs at the slowest stage plus latch, not the average or the sum. For n tasks the count is k + n − 1, so 500 tasks in a 4-stage pipe is 503 cycles, not 504. Classify data hazards by the shared register and the order it is written and read, never by the instruction name.

blocks.big: "Clock = the slowest stage + latch. For n tasks it is (k + n − 1) cycles."
blocks.sub: Speedup tops out at k stages. Name a data hazard by the register order: RAW (read after write, the real one, eased by forwarding), WAR, WAW. A long execute pushes everything behind it; a stall is a bubble.

title: Memory and Cache
lead: The memory hierarchy carries the largest single block of objective questions, and cache mapping is the most examined calculation on the whole course. It looks fiddly, so we do it as a programme: many tiny steps, and you check each one before moving on. By the end the cache split will be the same four moves every time.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do
the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a
time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: Memory is arranged in levels, fastest to slowest: registers, then cache, then main memory, then secondary storage (disk or SSD).
frames.ask: Of those four, which is the fastest?

frames.teach:
Picture it as your workspace: the few things in
your hands (registers), the book open on your desk (cache), the shelf beside you (main memory), and
the library across campus (disk). You keep what you use most closest, because reaching further
costs time.
frames.ask:
As you climb toward registers, does memory get cheaper or dearer per
bit?

frames.teach:
Climbing up, memory gets faster, smaller, and more
expensive per bit. The reason there are levels at all is a trade-off: you cannot have fast, big and
cheap at once.
frames.ask: So which level has the highest cost per bit?

frames.teach: Now the two kinds of RAM. SRAM (static RAM) is built from flip-flops: fast, needs no refresh, but costly and low density.
frames.ask: Given it is fast but costly, which level is SRAM used for?

frames.teach: DRAM (dynamic RAM) is built from capacitors: dense and cheap, but slower and it needs periodic refresh, so it is used for main memory. (ROM and Flash are non-volatile; RAM, cache and DRAM are volatile, lost on power off.)
frames.ask: Which kind of RAM has to be refreshed?

frames.teach: Two facts the MCQs love: the MAR (memory address register) holds the address being accessed; and access time is how long one access takes, while cycle time is the minimum gap between the starts of two accesses.
frames.ask: A device with 60 ns access and 90 ns cycle can start a new access how often?

frames.teach: (the cycle time, not the access time). Now, why does a small nearby cache help at all? Because programs are predictable, a habit called locality of reference. It comes in two kinds.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Temporal locality: a location used now is likely used again soon (think of a loop counter, read over and over).
frames.ask:
Reusing the same location again
soon is which locality?

frames.teach: Spatial locality: once a location is used, nearby ones are likely used next (stepping through an array). That is exactly why the cache copies a whole block at a time, not one lonely byte.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Two limits to know by name. The memory wall is the widening gap between fast CPUs and slow memory, which is why a processor can still wait on data despite a big cache. Virtual memory lets a program use an address space larger than the physical RAM, with a memory management unit (MMU) translating the addresses.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now the cache sum itself, gently. Picture the cache as a wall of numbered hooks (the lines), each big enough to hold one block, a short run of consecutive bytes copied from memory together. Far more blocks exist in memory than there are hooks, so many blocks compete for the same hook.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: When the CPU names an address, that address answers three questions, and that is exactly why it splits into three fields. The first, from the low bits, is the offset.
frames.ask:
Which one thing does the offset pick out: which byte in the block,
which hook, or which block?

frames.teach: The middle bits are the index (or set): which hook the block hangs on. The high bits are the tag: which of the many blocks sharing that hook is actually here, stored beside the block and compared on every access.
frames.ask: A tag that matches means what?

frames.teach: (no match is a miss). Now the sizes, in order. Address bits = log2(main memory size). Offset = log2(block size).
frames.ask: A 16-byte block needs how many offset bits?

frames.teach: (log216 = 4). Number of lines = cache size / block size. Index bits (direct mapped) = log2(lines).
frames.ask: A direct-mapped cache with 64 lines needs how many index bits?

frames.teach: (log264 = 6). For a k-way set associative cache, sets = lines / k and set bits = log2(sets); fully associative has no index at all (any block on any hook). Whatever is left over is the tag: tag bits = address bits − index (or set) − offset. The tag directory = lines × tag bits.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Last, the average memory access time (AMAT), with hit ratio h, cache time Tc and memory time Tm. Hierarchical (cache first): AMAT = Tc + (1 − h) × Tm. Simultaneous (both at once): AMAT = h × Tc + (1 − h) × Tm.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach:
That is the whole method: address bits from the
memory, offset from the block, lines from cache over block, tag is whatever is left, then the tag
directory and AMAT. Now watch it on real numbers in the three worked examples below, then drill the
six extra caches with a card over each row.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.tag: the cache split on one card
blocks.html:
• Address bits = log2(main memory size).
  • Offset = log2(block size). It picks the byte inside a block.
  • Number of lines = cache size / block size.
  • Index bits (direct) = log2(lines). For a k-way set associative cache, sets = lines / k and set bits = log2(sets). Fully associative has no index at all.
  • Tag bits = address bits − index (or set) bits − offset bits. The tag directory is lines × tag bits.
Hierarchical (cache first): AMAT = Tc + (1 − h) × Tm.   Simultaneous (both at once): AMAT = h × Tc + (1 − h) × Tm.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Main memory 64 KB, cache 1 KB, block 16 B, direct mapped. Find the address split and the tag-directory size.
blocks.working:
Address = log2(64 KB) = log2(2¹⁶)     = 16 bits
Offset  = log2(16)                     = 4 bits
Lines   = cache/block = 1024/16 = 64
Index   = log2(64)                     = 6 bits
Tag     = 16 - 6 - 4                   = 6 bits
Tag dir = lines x tag = 64 x 6 = 384 bits = 48 bytes
blocks.answer: Offset 4, index 6, tag 6; tag directory 384 bits (48 bytes).
blocks.redo: Now redo it: address from the memory size, offset from the block, lines from cache over block, and the tag is whatever is left. This works for any numbers.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Hit rate 80%, cache time 5 ns, memory time 100 ns. Find the AMAT both ways.
blocks.working:
Simultaneous = h.Tc + (1-h).Tm = 0.8x5 + 0.2x100 = 4 + 20 = 24 ns
Hierarchical =   Tc + (1-h).Tm =    5 + 0.2x100 = 5 + 20 = 25 ns
blocks.answer:
Simultaneous 24 ns, hierarchical 25 ns. Hierarchical pays the cache time
on every access, so it is a touch slower here.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.tag: the revision deck's six extra caches
blocks.problem:
The lecturer's revision deck sets six more cache problems (Examples 2 and 3 of each mapping). They are not on the 2025/2026 paper, so drill the method on these fresh numbers. Cover a row, rebuild it from the four sizes, then check.
