Direct, 128 KB / 4 KB / 32 B5index 75128640 bits (80 bytes)
Direct, 1 MB / 8 KB / 64 B6index 77128896 bits (112 bytes)
Fully assoc, 256 KB / 4 KB / 32 B5none131281664 bits (208 bytes)
Fully assoc, 2 MB / 16 KB / 64 B6none152563840 bits (480 bytes)
4-way, 512 KB / 8 KB / 32 B5set 682562048 bits (256 bytes)
8-way, 4 MB / 32 KB / 64 B6set 6105125120 bits (640 bytes)
blocks.answer:
The lines are set by cache over block; the tag directory grows as the
mapping gets more associative, because dropping the index lengthens the tag on every line.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) Order fastest to slowest: registers, cache, main memory, secondary. (2) SRAM versus DRAM in one line? (3) Reusing the same location soon is which locality? (4) A program using more address space than physical RAM uses what? (5) Which memory has the highest cost per bit?
blocks.answer: (1) registers, cache, main memory, secondary. (2) SRAM = flip-flops, fast, no refresh; DRAM = capacitors, dense, needs refresh. (3) temporal (nearby locations would be spatial). (4) virtual memory. (5) registers.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: Keep the units straight: offset comes from the block size, lines from cache over block. For set associative, divide lines by the ways to get sets before taking the log, and the bits you save on the index move into the tag. Temporal locality is "same place, later"; spatial is "nearby places".

blocks.big: "Offset, index, tag = which byte, which hook, which block."
blocks.sub: Offset = log2(block), lines = cache ÷ block, index = log2(lines), and the tag is whatever is left. AMAT = Tc + (1 − h) × Tm. Registers are fastest and dearest; DRAM needs refresh, SRAM does not.

title: RISC, CISC and the Rest
lead: Two design philosophies, plus the loose theory ideas the objective test dips into. Mostly describing and comparing, so we do it as a short programme: one small contrast at a time, then check. Get the contrasts clean and these are fast, reliable marks.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do
the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a
time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: An instruction set can be designed with two opposite philosophies. The first is CISC (complex instruction set computer): many, powerful, variable-length instructions, some doing a lot of work each (even direct memory-to-memory operations).
frames.ask: Does CISC have few or many instructions?

frames.teach: Because each instruction does so much, CISC programs are short, but the hardware is complex, instructions take several cycles, and it is harder to pipeline. Its instructions can resemble high-level language constructs, which eases the compiler. It suited the old days of slow, expensive memory.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: The opposite is RISC (reduced instruction set computer): few, simple, fixed-length instructions, each ideally one cycle.
frames.ask:
Are RISC
instructions fixed-length or variable-length?

frames.teach: RISC touches memory only through load and store (a load-store design), keeps many registers, and uses hardwired control. Programs are longer, but the hardware is simple, fast, and pipelines cleanly. It minimises chip area and power and leans on the compiler.
frames.ask:
So which philosophy pipelines more
easily, RISC or CISC?

frames.teach:
(simple fixed-length instructions flow through the
pipeline cleanly). One quick sort for the exam:
frames.ask:
variable-length instruction
formats go with RISC or CISC?

frames.teach:
(RISC is fixed-length). The card just below lays the two
side by side. Examples to recognise: RISC is ARM, MIPS, SPARC, PowerPC; CISC is Intel x86, VAX, the
Motorola 68000.
frames.ask: Read on to the loose ideas the MCQs also test.

frames.teach: SIMD (single instruction, multiple data): one instruction acts on many data items at once, to speed up data-parallel work like graphics and matrices.
frames.ask: Why does SIMD exist?

frames.teach: Domain-specific architecture: a processor tailored to one job (say the matrix work in AI) can be far more efficient than a general-purpose one for that job.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Abstraction: layering the design, with the ISA as the key layer, lets the hardware and software teams work independently while staying compatible.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Backward compatibility: keeping a stable ISA while the organization underneath evolves is what lets twenty-year-old software still run on new chips.
frames.ask: What one thing gives backward compatibility across processor generations?

frames.teach: (with the organization evolving underneath). Last one, a wording the test likes: architecture versus engineering. Computer architecture is the conceptual, operational design; computer engineering is the broader design, build and integration of the hardware.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: You have now met every skill the exam tests. What is left is proof: turn the page and work the MCQ bank a whole topic at a time with the answers covered, going back to any skill you miss, then sit the 2025/2026 paper at the very back under exam conditions.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.tag: RISC versus CISC, side by side
blocks.html:
RISCCISC
Few, simple, fixed-length instructionsMany, complex, variable-length
Mostly one cycle each; pipelines wellSeveral cycles; harder to pipeline
Load-store; many registersMemory-to-memory; fewer registers

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: a. i) Computer Systems are designed using two closely related but distinct concepts which are Computer Architecture and Computer Organization. Differentiate between these concepts. 2mks ii) Compare Von Neumann Architecture and Harvard Architecture. Include a diagram for each. 3mks

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
i) Differentiate computer architecture from computer organization.

Computer architecture is defined as the functional design and logical structure of the computer system as the programmer sees it: the instruction set, the data types, the addressing modes and the register organization. It answers the question "What does the computer do?" and serves as the blueprint for the system.

Computer organization is defined as the operational units and their interconnections that realize (carry out) that architecture: the control signals, the buses, the memory technology used and the cache. It answers the question "How does the computer do it?" A useful likeness: architecture is the building's design, organization is the actual construction of the building.

ii) Compare Von Neumann and Harvard architecture, with a diagram for each.

Von Neumann architecture is defined as a design that uses a single (shared) area of memory, reached over one bus, for both the program instructions and the data those instructions act on. It is simple to build, but the shared path is a bottleneck (an instruction fetch and a data access cannot happen at the same instant).

Harvard architecture is defined as a design that uses separate memories and separate buses for instructions and data, which lets it fetch an instruction and read data at the same time (a form of parallelism), at the cost of duplicating the address, data and control lines.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: b. A computer manufacturer is evaluating whether to replace a non-pipelined processor with a five-stage pipelined processor. The processor executes the following instruction mix: Arithmetic – 40%, Memory Access – 35%, Branch – 20%, Floating Point – 5%. The Non-pipelined processor clock cycle is 25ns. Pipelined processor stage times are: IF – 5ns, ID – 4ns, EX – 6ns, MEM – 5ns and WB – 4ns. Furthermore, Pipeline register overhead is 1 ns. Branch instructions incur a two-cycle penalty, Floating-point instructions has three cycles for EX stage, Memory accesses experience cache misses 10% of the time, adding four extra cycles. The program contains 20 million instructions. i) Determine the pipelined clock cycle. 1mk ii) Calculate the actual CPI. 2mks iii) Determine the actual execution time. 1mk iv) Compute the speedup over the non-pipelined processor. 1mk v) Explain why the speedup differs from the theoretical maximum. 1mk

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
Given mix arithmetic 40%, memory 35%, branch 20%, floating point 5% ; five stage times 5, 4, 6, 5, 4 ns ; register overhead 1 ns ; non-pipelined clock 25 ns ; IC = 20 000 000 ; branch adds a 2-cycle penalty, floating point adds 4 extra cycles, a memory access misses 10% of the time adding 4 more.
Find pipelined clock, actual CPI, execution time, speedup, and why it is short of the max
Formula clock = slowest stage + overhead · actual CPI = 1 + Σ(fraction × extra cycles) · time = IC × CPI × T · speedup = time(non-pipe) / time(pipe)

The stem is dense and does not say whether each penalty is extra or total, so state the reading: base CPI 1; branch +2; memory +(2 + 0.10×4) = 2.4; floating point +4; arithmetic +0.

Clock  = max(5,4,6,5,4) + overhead
       = 6 + 1 = 7 ns

CPI    = 1                (base, one per cycle)
       + 0.20 x 2         (branch)
       + 0.35 x 2.4       (memory: 2 + 0.10x4)
       + 0.05 x 4         (floating point)
       + 0.40 x 0         (arithmetic)
       = 1 + 0.40 + 0.84 + 0.20
       = 2.44

Time   = IC x CPI x T
       = 20,000,000 x 2.44 x 7 ns = 0.3416 s
Non-pipe = 20,000,000 x 25 ns    = 0.5 s
Speedup  = 0.5 / 0.3416          = 1.46
blocks.answer: Clock 7 ns; CPI 2.44; time 0.3416 s; speedup 1.46. (v) It is far below the ideal 5 because the branch, floating-point and cache-miss penalties and the register overhead all raise the CPI above 1.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: c. A spacecraft telemetry system uses a 16-bit processor to transmit environmental measurements. The following values are to be stored - Temperature = -182; Pressure = 487; Altitude = -1023. The processor uses 2's complement representation for signed integers. i) Determine the range of values representable in a 16-bit two's complement system. Indicate whether the given numbers fall within the range of value 2mks ii) Represent each value in: Binary and Hexadecimal 3mks iii) Demonstrate how the processor uses two's complement to compute 2mks (−182) + 487

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
Given 16-bit two's complement ; Temperature −182, Pressure 487, Altitude −1023
Find the range and whether each fits ; each in binary and hex ; (−182) + 487
Formula range = −215 to 215 − 1 · negative = invert the positive and add 1 · group 4 bits per hex digit
Range: -2¹⁵ to 2¹⁵ - 1  =  -32768 to 32767   (all three fit)

487  =  0000 0001 1110 0111  =  01E7

-182:  +182  =  0000 0000 1011 0110
     invert  =  1111 1111 0100 1001
        + 1  =  1111 1111 0100 1010  =  FF4A

-1023: +1023 =  0000 0011 1111 1111
     invert  =  1111 1100 0000 0000
        + 1  =  1111 1100 0000 0001  =  FC01

(-182) + 487:
     1111 1111 0100 1010
   + 0000 0001 1110 0111
   ---------------------
   1 0000 0001 0011 0001   drop the carry off the top
     0000 0001 0011 0001   =  256+32+16+1  =  305
blocks.answer: Range −32768 to 32767 (all fit). 487 = 01E7, −182 = FF4A, −1023 = FC01. (−182) + 487 = 305: the machine adds the patterns and gets the right signed answer.

blocks.printed:
d. A processor executes one million(1M) instructions distributed as follows.
Addressing ModePercentageCycles
Register40%1
Immediate20%1
Direct15%2
Indirect10%4
Indexed10%3
Relative5%2
i) Compute the average CPI 2mks ii) Determine total clock cycles. 1mk iii) If indirect addressing is optimized to 2 cycles, compute the new CPI. 1mk iv) Evaluate the performance improvement. 2mks

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
Given 1,000,000 instructions ; per-mode share and cycles as tabled
Find average CPI, total cycles, new CPI after optimising indirect, improvement
Formula CPI = Σ(fraction × cycles) · total = IC × CPI · improvement = (old − new)/old
Avg CPI = 0.40x1 + 0.20x1 + 0.15x2 + 0.10x4 + 0.10x3 + 0.05x2
        = 0.40 + 0.20 + 0.30 + 0.40 + 0.30 + 0.10
        = 1.70

Total cycles = 1,000,000 x 1.70 = 1,700,000

Indirect 4 -> 2:  new CPI = 1.70 - 0.10x4 + 0.10x2
                          = 1.70 - 0.20 = 1.50

Improvement = (1.70 - 1.50) / 1.70 = 0.20 / 1.70 = 11.76%

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: a. Assume a computer has 32-bit addresses. Each block stores 16 words. A direct-mapped cache has 256 blocks. In which block (line) of the cache (decimal value) would you look for each of the following addresses? Addresses are given in hexadecimal for convenience. 4mks i. CA2DFC12 ii. F24F25FF iii. 24BBABCD iv. C1D9EEF2

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
Given 32-bit address ; 16 words per block ; direct-mapped, 256 blocks
Find the cache line each hex address maps to, in decimal
Formula offset = log2(words/block) ; index = log2(lines) ; the index field IS the line
offset = log2(16) = 4 bits    (one hex digit)
index  = log2(256) = 8 bits   (two hex digits)
So: drop the last hex digit (offset), read the next two (the line):

  CA2DFC1|2   ->  C1  =  193
  F24F25F|F   ->  5F  =  95

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: b. Consider the following code segment executed on a classic five-stage RISC processor. I1: LW R1,0(R2) I2: ADD R3,R1,R4 I3: SUB R5,R3,R6 I4: SW R5,8(R2) I5: BEQ R5,R0,LABEL I6: MUL R7,R5,R8 Assume: • forwarding is available • branch resolved in EX stage • load-use hazards require one stall • multiplier occupies EX for three cycles • separate instruction and data caches i) Identify and explain every pipeline hazard. 5mks ii) Draw the pipeline timing diagram 2mks iii) Determine the total execution cycles 1mk iv) Suggest any two hardware improvements that would reduce stalls. 1mk

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
Given six instructions on a classic 5-stage RISC pipeline ; forwarding on ; branch resolved in EX ; load-use costs 1 stall ; MUL holds EX for 3 cycles ; separate caches
Find the hazards, the timing diagram, the total cycles, two improvements
Formula ideal = (k + n − 1) cycles, then add every stall: 1 per load-use, and (EX cycles − 1) per multi-cycle execute

Hazards

I1→I2 is a load-use RAW (R1 not ready until MEM, so I2 stalls one cycle). I2→I3, I3→I4, I3→I5, I3→I6 are ordinary RAW hazards hidden by forwarding. I6's multiply holds EX for three cycles, adding two extra at the end. Structural hazards are avoided by the separate caches.

Timing diagram (one stall, then the long multiply)

Cyc12345678910111213
I1 LWIFIDEXMEWB
I2 ADDIFID--EXMEWB
I3 SUBIF--IDEXMEWB
I4 SWIFIDEXMEWB
I5 BEQIFIDEXMEWB
I6 MULIFIDEXEXEXMEWB
blocks.answer: One load-use stall (the -- in cycle 4) plus two extra multiply cycles give a total of 13 cycles (a clean run of 6 would be 5 + 6 − 1 = 10). Two improvements: add more forwarding paths, and pipeline or duplicate the multiplier.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: c. A processor has the following configuration: Main memory is 1 GB; Cache is 512 KB; Block size is 128 bytes and it is a 4-way Set Associative cache. i) Determine the total number of cache blocks. 1mk ii) Determine the number of sets. 1mk iii) Construct the complete address format. 1mk iv) If the hit rate is 96%, cache access time is 2 ns, and main memory access time is 80 ns, calculate the Average Memory Access Time (AMAT). 2mks v) Discuss how increasing associativity beyond four ways might affect performance. 2mks

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
Given main memory 1 GB ; cache 512 KB ; block 128 B ; 4-way ; h = 0.96, Tc = 2 ns, Tm = 80 ns
Find blocks, sets, the address format, the AMAT
Formula blocks = cache/block ; sets = blocks/ways ; tag = addr − set − offset ; AMAT = Tc + (1−h)×Tm
Blocks = 512 KB / 128 B = 2¹⁹ / 2⁷ = 4096
Sets   = 4096 / 4 = 1024
Address = 1 GB = 2³⁰ -> 30 bits
  offset = log2(128) = 7
  set    = log2(1024) = 10
  tag    = 30 - 10 - 7 = 13
AMAT = Tc + (1-h)Tm = 2 + 0.04 x 80 = 2 + 3.2 = 5.2 ns
blocks.answer: 4096 blocks; 1024 sets; address tag 13 / set 10 / offset 7; AMAT 5.2 ns. (v) More ways cuts conflict misses but needs more tag comparators, so beyond a point it adds cost and delay for little gain.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: a. A computer system has the following characteristics: • Main memory = 64 MB • Cache memory = 128 KB • Block size = 64 bytes i) Determine the number of cache lines 1½mks ii) For Direct Mapping, determine: Number of index bits; Number of tag bits; Number of offset bits 1½mks iii) For a 4-way Set Associative Cache, determine: Number of sets; Number of set index bits; Number of tag bits 1½mks iv) Explain why fully associative mapping eliminates conflict misses but introduces another performance challenge. 1½mks

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
Given main memory 64 MB ; cache 128 KB ; block 64 B
Find lines ; direct fields ; 4-way fields ; the fully-associative trade-off
Formula lines = cache/block ; offset = log2(block) ; tag = addr − index(or set) − offset
Lines = 128 KB / 64 B = 2¹⁷ / 2⁶ = 2¹¹ = 2048
Address = 64 MB = 2²⁶ -> 26 bits ; offset = log2(64) = 6

Direct: index = log2(2048) = 11 ; tag = 26 - 11 - 6 = 9
4-way : sets = 2048/4 = 512 ; set = log2(512) = 9 ; tag = 26 - 9 - 6 = 11
blocks.answer: 2048 lines. Direct: index 11, tag 9, offset 6. 4-way: set 9, tag 11, offset 6. (iv) Fully associative lets any block go in any line, so no conflict misses, but every line's tag must be searched, which is slow and costly.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: b. A 5-stage pipelined processor has instruction fetch (IF), Instruction decode (ID), Operand Fetch (OF), Execute (Ex) and Write Back (WB) stages. The IF, ID, OF and WB stages take 1 clock cycle each for any instruction. The PO stage take 1 cycle for ADD and SUB instructions, 3 clock cycles for MUL instruction and 6 clock cycles for DIV instruction respectively. Operand forwarding is used in the pipeline. Draw the cycle diagram and determine the number of cycles needed to execute the following sequence of instructions: i. When Operand forwarding is used 4½mks ii. When Operand forwarding is not used 5½mks I1 MUL R2, R0, R1 ; R2 ← R0 X R1 I2 DIV R5, R3, R4 ; R5 ← R3/R4 I3 ADD R2, R5, R2 ; R2 ← R5 + R2 I4 SUB R5, R2, R6 ; R5 ← R2 – R6

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
Given 5 stages IF, ID, OF, EX, WB, one cycle each except EX = 1 (ADD/SUB), 3 (MUL), 6 (DIV) ; four instructions ; do it with and without forwarding
Find the cycle diagram and total cycles for each case
Formula no single formula once EX is multi-cycle: lay the schedule out cycle by cycle, a long EX blocks those behind it, then read the total off the last write-back

The paper prints "PO stage", struck through in pen to EX. Instructions: I1 MUL R2,R0,R1 ; I2 DIV R5,R3,R4 ; I3 ADD R2,R5,R2 (needs R5 from I2 and R2 from I1) ; I4 SUB R5,R2,R6 (needs R2 from I3). Read each cell as the stage that instruction is in that cycle; "--" is a stall.

(i) With operand forwarding

Instr123456789101112131415
I1 MULIFIDOFEXEXEXWB
I2 DIVIFIDOF----EXEXEXEXEXEXWB
I3 ADDIFID----OF----------EXWB
I4 SUBIF----ID----------OFEXWB

The DIV holds EX for six cycles (7 to 12) and blocks everything behind it. With forwarding, I3 takes R5 straight from I2's EX and runs at cycle 13, and I4 takes R2 from I3 and runs at 14, so the last write-back is at cycle 15.

(ii) Without operand forwarding

Instr1234567891011121314151617
I1 MULIFIDOFEXEXEXWB
I2 DIVIFIDOF----EXEXEXEXEXEXWB
I3 ADDIFID----OF------------EXWB
I4 SUBIF----ID--------------OFEXWB

Without forwarding, I3 must wait for I2's write-back before it can read R5 (one cycle later, EX at 14), and I4 likewise waits for I3, so the last write-back slips to cycle 17.
blocks.answer: Total = 15 cycles with forwarding, 17 cycles without. Forwarding saved 2 cycles here.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: c. i) State Amdahl's law' 2mks ii) Assume in hypothetical system cache is 10 times faster than main memory and CPU accesses the cache 85% of the time. Using Amdahl's law, calculate the overall speed up of the system. 2mks

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
Given cache 10 times faster than memory ; used 85% of the time
Find state Amdahl's law, then the overall speedup
Formula S = 1 / ((1−f) + f/s), with f the sped-up fraction and s its speedup

Amdahl's law states that the overall speedup obtainable by improving one part of a system is limited by the fraction of the total time that part is actually used: even if that part is made infinitely fast, the speedup can never exceed 1/(1−f), where f is the fraction of the time that is sped up.

f = 0.85 (cache hits), s = 10
S = 1 / ((1 - 0.85) + 0.85/10)
  = 1 / (0.15 + 0.085)
  = 1 / 0.235
  = 4.26
blocks.answer: S = 4.26, far below 10, because the 15% of slow accesses dominate.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: a. Consider three (3) floating point numbers X, Y and Z stored in registers based on the IEEE 754 Single precision floating point format. X = C1400000h, Y = 42100000h, Z = 41400000h Convert X, Y and Z to decimal numbers and determine which of the following is true. 9mks i. (Y-Z)>0 ii. X + Z = 0 iii. Z= X + Y

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
Given X = C1400000h, Y = 42100000h, Z = 41400000h, IEEE-754 single precision
Find each in decimal, then which claim is true
Formula value = (−1)s × 1.M × 2(E − 127), where s = sign bit, M = mantissa, E = exponent field
X = C1400000 = 1 10000010 100 0000...
    sign 1 (neg); exp 130, e = 3; 1.100... = 1.5
    X = -1.5 x 2³ = -12

Y = 42100000 = 0 10000100 001 0000...
    sign 0; exp 132, e = 5; 1.001... = 1.125
    Y = 1.125 x 2⁵ = 36

Z = 41400000 = 0 10000010 100 0000...
    sign 0; exp 130, e = 3; 1.5
    Z = +1.5 x 2³ = 12

(Y - Z) = 36 - 12 = 24 > 0   TRUE
X + Z   = -12 + 12 = 0       TRUE
Z = X + Y ?  12 = -12+36=24  FALSE
blocks.answer: X = −12, Y = 36, Z = 12. (i) true, (ii) true, (iii) false.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: b. Use a Zero, One, Two and Three address instruction formats to write a Pentium 4 assembly language program segment for the expression below. For each format determine the number of bytes required. X = ((A * B) +C/D)/(F*G+J*K) 8mks

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
On the sheet the sentence "For each format determine the number of bytes required" is struck through in pen, so in that one sitting only the four programs were wanted. But the PRINTED paper asks for the byte counts too, so here is both: the programs, then the byte count for each format. If the strike is not on your paper, you have the full answer; if it is, the totals cost four lines and cannot lose marks.

Three-address (numerator, then denominator, then divide):

MUL  R1, A, B      ; R1 = A*B
DIV  R2, C, D      ; R2 = C/D
ADD  R1, R1, R2    ; numerator
MUL  R2, F, G
MUL  R3, J, K
ADD  R2, R2, R3    ; denominator
DIV  X,  R1, R2    ; X = numerator / denominator

Two-address: MOV/op with the destination doubling as a source. One-address: work through the accumulator (LOAD, op, STORE). Zero-address: a stack (PUSH the eight operands, then each ADD/MUL/DIV pops two and pushes the result, finally POP X).

Byte count for each format (the printed part, worked)

Given the paper gives no field sizes, so state the usual convention: opcode = 1 byte, each address = 2 bytes
Formula bytes per instruction = opcode + (address fields × 2) · total = instruction count × bytes per instruction
FormatInstructionsBytes
3-address77 × (1 + 3×2) = 7 × 7 = 49
2-address1212 × (1 + 2×2) = 12 × 5 = 60
1-address1717 × (1 + 1×2) = 17 × 3 = 51
0-address168 pushes×3 + 1 pop×3 + 7 ops×1 = 34
blocks.answer: Same X in all four formats. Byte totals 49, 60, 51 and 34 for 3, 2, 1 and 0-address. Fewer address fields shortens each instruction but needs more of them, so the totals stay close, and 0-address is smallest here because its operation instructions carry no address at all.

blocks.printed: c. Calculate the memory requirement of an image whose dimension is 17.12 inches by 9.45 inches at resolution 250 dpi. Express your answer in Megabyte 3mks

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
Given 17.12 in by 9.45 in at 250 dpi ; 1 bit per pixel
Find the memory in megabytes
Formula pixels = inches × dpi (both ways) ; bytes = pixels × bits / 8 ; MB = bytes / 1024 / 1024
pixels across = 17.12 x 250 = 4280
pixels down   =  9.45 x 250 = 2362.5
total pixels  = 4280 x 2362.5 = 10,111,500
bytes = 10,111,500 / 8 = 1,263,937.5
MB    = 1,263,937.5 / 1024 / 1024 = 1.21 MB

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: a. Represent the following -1240.56 using Single Precision IEEE format for floating point numbers. 6mks

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
Given −1240.56, single precision
Find the 32-bit pattern (and its hex)
Formula sign ; normalise |x| to 1.M × 2e ; exp field = e + 127 ; mantissa M = f to 23 bits
sign = 1  (negative)
1240.56 in binary = 1.0011011000100011110101... x 2¹⁰

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: b. Consider a pipeline having 4 phases with duration 60, 50, 90 and 80 ns. Given latch delay is 10 ns. Calculate- i. Pipeline cycle time 1mk ii. Non-pipeline execution time 1mk iii. Speed up ratio 1mk iv. Pipeline time for 500 tasks 1mk v. Sequential time for 500 tasks 1mk

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
Given 4 phases 60, 50, 90, 80 ns ; latch 10 ns ; 500 tasks
Find cycle time, one-task time, speedup, and the times for 500 tasks
Formula cycle = slowest + latch ; pipe(n) = (k + n − 1)×cycle ; seq(n) = n × Σphases ; speedup = Σphases / cycle
Cycle    = max(60,50,90,80) + 10 = 90 + 10 = 100 ns
One task = 60 + 50 + 90 + 80 = 280 ns
Speedup  = 280 / 100 = 2.8
Pipe 500 = (4 + 500 - 1) x 100 = 503 x 100 = 50,300 ns
Seq 500  = 500 x 280 = 140,000 ns
blocks.answer: Cycle 100 ns; one task 280 ns; speedup 2.8; 500 tasks pipelined 50,300 ns vs sequential 140,000 ns.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: c. Explain the following terms 3mks i. Locality of reference ii. Temporal locality

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
i) Locality of reference is defined as the tendency of a program to keep accessing the same small set of memory locations over a short period, a consequence of loops and subroutines; it is why a small fast cache can satisfy most accesses.

ii) Temporal (time) locality is defined as: if a memory location is accessed, it is very likely to be accessed again soon (the same instruction or variable reused). Its partner, spatial (space) locality, is defined as: if a location is accessed, the nearby addresses are very likely to be accessed next (as when stepping through an array).
